interactions.title: Rhodar remembers the bargain that freed him
lines: DM: We begin in the darkness as we catch a glimpse into the mind of Lord Rhodar von Glauer, looking at the sad creatures bumbling in the dark before him in another misguided attempt to take his power, he assumes. Watching them, he thinks back. He can still remember his days among the living. He joined the Eyes of Vedmakov out of a sense of patriotism, he supposes. Misguided, it turned out. In those days the Rodnya Okolov was strong. The eyes and the shield, people said, Okolov and Morozmir, the watchers and the protectors, the heart of the defense of Ursk against the dragons of the North, who are always seeking to reclaim their power, to rise again in another great host, to see another Vimfrost take all the north. He took to the magic of Okolov so easily. Even now the watcher's magic flows through him. Those fool adventurers probably don't realize he's been watching them since they set foot on Drachen's Peak, waiting patiently. They have shown skill and cleverness, though. They'll make good lieutenants. No slow cold death in the snow for them, their minds consumed by Putrid Agnes. The death of servitude in his army is what they deserve and what they'll get.

DM: With his sight, he advanced quickly. A boy from a tiny village in the foothills, from nothing really, was soon taking the oath and the binding, even being talked about as the next leader of the Rodnya Okolov. The one thing he misses sometimes: the vast scope of his sight back then, powered by the krev, watching the whole of Ursk from the high towers in Vedmakov, seeing the plumes of magic, the occasional hole in the Morozmir wards that signaled a fool to be dealt with, being able to close his eyes and still see the pulsing waves of krev flowing across the land. That was something.

DM: But how little he knew then, until he took the final step and realized it was all a lie. His power was not his, was never his. It was always Ursk's, and only for Ursk. Rodnya Morozmir was too clever. Krev, the arcane upwelling, now a millstone, a noose around his neck. He had come from nothing and thought he was growing strong, but it was all for naught. He was instead growing into a servant, utterly bound to the people who sacrificed for him. He was not free, not even a little. Not free, even though he was the leader of the strongest Rodnya in Ursk. He could feel the iron walls of duty closing around him, changing him, infiltrating his mind, and he had to escape.

DM: Somewhere there had to be a solution. It was a little nagging thing that gave him the answer. A petty hedge witch who had made some kind of promise to a devil, she knew not who, but it gave her power and strength outside the krev. She was nothing, a pointless plaything for the fiend. He, though, was far from nothing.

DM: The petty hedge witch had to die, of course, but in her death a deal could be made. Freedom and eternal life, the only cost a price he would never pay, for he never planned to die. He even grew to love the taste of blood.
DM: He grins in the darkness, eager for the new blood to fill his ranks.

interactions.title: The third jade fragment reveals Apollyon’s weakening bonds

DM: You're standing in the dream world in a vast domed room. A beam of sunlight shines through the oculus, the circular opening at the crown of the vast ceiling, reflecting from the polished marble floor, somehow lighting the room and sparkling off countless silver stars inside the ceiling. You can feel energy flowing around you, deep, ancient magic of this place that flows beneath your feet.

DM: Some distance away, not immediately nearby but close enough to grasp, you can feel the rough, feel the rough chains of the magic woven by Cha'mutte, the binding of Apollyon. It takes no effort at all to divert a portion of the magic flowing beneath your feet to pull the chains tight. You reach into the chains and poke around and probe at them and feel the layers and layers and layers of traps and bonds, more powerful magic than even you could create, but not so powerful that you cannot maintain it, hold on to these chains.

DM: Hardest to hold on to are the magical bonds that keep Apollyon powerless, the, the ties that wrap around him, that keep him unable to access his magical power, that keep them unable to reach out and connect to the soul jar that holds his life force. This is the magic that should have, that would have killed him if it were not for careful preparation, hiding his life force even from Cha'mutte.

DM: Somewhat easier to hold onto, but still challenging, are the physical bonds, the chains that tie him to his final resting place, that keep the powerless corpse of Apollyon physically immobile in his tomb.

DM: Simplest of all are the locks and wards around the tomb itself, requiring really no effort at all to maintain. Should all else fail, these are the last, last resort, for Apollyon cannot truly regain his power till he is physically reunited with the soulstone that holds his life force and is once again able to feed it the souls of the dead.
DM: Suddenly, as you pull all of these chains and locks and bonds in your hand, time ruptures, and the vision splinters.

DM: You see the past, the present, the future all at once. Magical bonds that keep Apollyon powerless and that chained him immobile to his tomb fracture, have been fractured for many years. The flow of energy shifts and is shifting now, and magic pours into Apollyon's tomb. Yet his soulstone is still trapped.

DM: The souls of the dead killed in Apollyon's name give him power. They pour into Drankor. They're still pouring into Drankor. Many, but too few, far too few. Hundreds only, when thousands or more would have been better.
DM: Still, hundreds are enough, maybe, to shatter the last wards and locks and be free. But it'll take time. Weeks to do it now, instead of instantaneously in the vision where thousands are dead.
DM: But the chains are breaking, will break, and as you watch, time running in all directions and the chains crack, the vision ends, and the jade fuses onto Kenzo's staff.
